cards.text: This is a psalm of David, and he opens with a big question for the LORD: who may abide in His tent and dwell on His holy mountain? Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer. You had me at "tent."

cards.question: David asks the LORD who may dwell on His holy mountain. True or false: David answers with a list of offerings to bring to the LORD's tent.

cards.text: First, the big picture: this person walks with integrity and practices righteousness. Same guy in the meeting as he is in the parking lot when somebody takes his spot. SAME GUY.

cards.question: The person who walks with integrity also speaks the truth. Where does David say that truth comes from?

cards.text: Then David turns to the tongue, and this person has no slander on it. He has never once sent the group chat text that starts with "I'm not trying to start anything, BUT…"

cards.question: David says the one who dwells on the LORD's holy mountain does no harm to his neighbor.
No slander on his tongue, no harm to his neighbor, no scorn on his friend. Who are all three of these about?

cards.text: Next, David gets to who this person looks up to. He despises the vile, so he is NOT out here giving the troublemakers a standing ovation.

cards.question: The one who despises the vile honors a different kind of person instead. Who?

cards.text: Now the tough one: this person made an oath, and keeping it is going to cost him. Like saying "Sure, I'll help you move" and THEN finding out it's a third floor walk-up with no elevator.

cards.question: Once his oath starts costing him, the person in Psalm 15 revises it.

cards.text: Then David gets to the wallet, friend. And this is right about where a lot of us start studying the ceiling real hard.

cards.question: When the one who dwells on the LORD's holy mountain lends his money, he lends it without ___.
The one who dwells on the LORD's holy mountain also refuses a bribe against the ___.

cards.text: And David brings it home. After that whole list, he has one last word about the one who does these things.

cards.question: What does David say about the one who does these things?

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'First, the big picture: this person walks with integrity and practices righteousness.' 'Same guy in the meeting as he is in the parking lot when somebody takes his spot.' 'SAME GUY.' Only the opening card can run to 3 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The question asks who the three lines are about. 'His own belongings' isn't a who, so it isn't the same kind of thing as the other two answers. It also stands out as the throwaway option, because the question already names 'neighbor' and 'friend.'

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The setup says 'keeping it is going to cost him,' which tells the baker he keeps the oath. That gives away card 11, which asks whether he revises it.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The only setup is 'David gets to the wallet.' Lending without interest, without contracts and without collateral are all equally believable generous acts, so the baker is guessing the next word of the line, not reasoning to it.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: No story card mentions a bribe, so the baker gets no setup for this question. Filling in 'innocent' over 'powerful' or 'foreigner' means guessing the wording of the line, not reasoning from context.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.
